title: UNIQUE constraints
description: `customers.email` has a UNIQUE constraint, so the database itself refuses to store two customers with the same email - even if you never checked for a duplicate yourself. Write an INSERT into `customers` that reuses an email already in the table (for example `ana.silva@example.com`) and watch Postgres reject it.
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: UNIQUE constraint

A UNIQUE constraint is a rule the table enforces on every write, not something your query has to check for itself - if you INSERT a row whose email column already exists elsewhere in the table, Postgres raises an error and nothing is written.
Write a normal INSERT INTO customers with values for every NOT NULL column, but set email to a value you already know is taken.
expected_behavior: The INSERT is rejected with a unique-constraint violation - the exercise passes when your query correctly fails.
solution: INSERT INTO customers (first_name, last_name, email, city, country, signup_date) VALUES ('Test', 'User', 'ana.silva@example.com', 'Lisbon', 'Portugal', '2024-01-01');
explanation: UNIQUE constraints are checked on every INSERT and UPDATE, independent of any application code - it's the database guaranteeing the rule instead of trusting every caller to remember it.
postgres_note: The error Postgres raises is a UniqueViolation naming the constraint (e.g. customers_email_key) - that name comes from the constraint you declared when the table was created.
